PASSO 1: o futuro simples se forma com o: STEP 1: the simple future is built from the whole infinitive — nothing gets dropped. That holds for all three groups (-ar, -er, -ir): «hablar», «comer», «vivir». STEP 2: add these endings to the infinitive: -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án. They're the same for all three groups. «Hablaré, hablarás, hablará, hablaremos, hablaréis, hablarán.» STEP 3: every form carries an accent except «nosotros»: «hablaré», «hablarás», «hablará», «hablaremos», «hablaréis», «hablarán». STEP 4: the pronoun «yo» and the others are usually dropped; the ending already tells you who. STEP 5: for the nearer future, everyday speech prefers the present or «ir a + infinitive» (lesson 30): «Mañana trabajo», «Mañana voy a trabajar». The simple future sounds firmer or more formal and shows up a lot in predictions, promises, and written text. STEP 6: uses of the future: plans («El año que viene estudiaré en Granada»), predictions («Mañana lloverá»), promises («Te llamaré esta noche»), and probability about the present («Serán las cinco», meaning "it must be five o'clock"). STEP 7: the future with «si» and the present: «Si estudias, aprobarás», with the present after «si». The future never follows «si»: you don't say «si estudiarás».
em português, o futuro do presente («fal: English has no built-in future tense form at all — it just drops "will" in front of the unchanged infinitive for every single person: "I will speak, you will speak, she will speak." There's no ending to memorize and no distinction by person or number. Spanish's future really is a tacked-on suffix on the full infinitive (-é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án), which means six different endings to learn where English gets by with one invariant word. Don't forget the accent either: without it, «hablara» is a completely different verb form, not the future.

Dez verbos que mudam o radical no futuro: Ten verbs that change the stem in the future
PASSO 1: alguns verbos comuns não usam o: STEP 1: some common verbs don't use the whole infinitive. But the endings are the usual ones: -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, -án. STEP 2: the first group drops the infinitive's vowel: «poder → podré», «saber → sabré», «querer → querré», «haber → habré». STEP 3: the second group swaps the vowel for a «d»: «tener → tendré», «venir → vendré», «poner → pondré», «salir → saldré». STEP 4: the third group is the most irregular, since it drops letters: «decir → diré», «hacer → haré». STEP 5: the verbs built from these follow the base verb: «contener → contendré», «mantener → mantendré», «deshacer → desharé». STEP 6: «haber» in the future shows up almost only as «habrá» (there will be), an impersonal form that's always singular: «Mañana habrá una fiesta», «Habrá muchas personas». STEP 7: the future gets used a lot with «querer» and «poder» in careful speech: «¿Podrás venir?», «No querrá hablar». STEP 8: every other verb is regular in the future, including the ones that are irregular in the present: «ir → iré», «ser → seré», «estar → estaré», «dar → daré», «ver → veré». Memorize the ten: tendré, haré, diré, podré, pondré, saldré, vendré, sabré, querré, habré.
em português também há verbos que mudam: English has nothing resembling a sound change here, since "will" never touches the verb at all — "will have," "will do," "will come" stay exactly as regular as any other verb after "will." So these ten changed stems aren't a pattern you can borrow from English; they're ten forms to simply memorize as a set, the same way you'd memorize an irregular past tense, just in a different slot.
Tomorrow I'll have an important meeting.
On Saturday we'll go out with some friends.
I'll tell you the truth when you get here.
On Friday there will be a party in the neighborhood.

Para que serve o futuro: previsões, prom: What the future is for: predictions, promises, and guesses
PASSO 1: previsão: o futuro descreve o q: STEP 1: prediction: the future describes what's expected to happen. «Mañana lloverá en el norte», «La semana que viene hará más frío». STEP 2: promise and firm decision: «Te lo prometo: estudiaré todos los días», «Mañana te llamaré». STEP 3: a soft command with a note of authority: «Mañana vendrás a las nueve», which isn't a question but a heads-up that barely leaves room to say no. Use it carefully. STEP 4: doubt or guessing about the present: «¿Dónde estará Ana?» (I wonder where Ana is) and «Estará en casa» (She must be home). This only works with the simple future. English actually does something similar with "will": "She'll be home by now" works as a guess about the present the same way «Estará en casa» does — so this particular use transfers more naturally than most of this lesson. STEP 5: use time markers to place the action: «mañana», «el año que viene», «dentro de una semana». «Dentro de» means "in," the same "in" as English "in an hour": «Llegaré dentro de una hora» is "I'll arrive in an hour." STEP 6: «en una hora» can also mean the same thing, but «dentro de» is the clearer choice. STEP 7: with «cuando» and the future, Spanish uses the present (subjunctive) in the «cuando» clause: «Cuando llegues, te llamaré» — you'll see why later; for now just learn the pattern as a fixed phrase. STEP 8: weather talk: «llover» (llueve, lloverá), «hacer sol / calor / frío / viento», «estar nublado».
em português, as previsões usam «vai cho: English predictions use "it's going to rain" or "it will rain" about as interchangeably as Spanish uses «va a llover» and «lloverá», so that part feels familiar.
